job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Daria Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake at seven in my student hall in Bradford, make tea, and go to my one-year master's in management accounting. Three days a week I'm in lectures, and on Saturdays I work the counter at a pharmacy for about 14 hours. The rest is studying and applying for jobs I mostly don't hear back from.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about where you've come from and how you got here.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a bachelor's in accounting at the same university and passed with an average mark, nothing special. I had no internship because I was working weekends to pay rent, and that's exactly what the firms ask about. My mum cleans offices at night and can't help with money, so I owe about 41,000 on student loans. I did the master's because the graduate schemes kept turning me down after the online tests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because maybe the fuss will die down and the firms will go back to hiring people. But I'd say it carefully at the pharmacy, because the pharmacist loves telling me how AI will take my job. Online I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing changes for me, and that's the problem. There are few junior accountancy jobs around Bradford even now, and I owe 41,000. Hype or not, Hype or not, I'm still stuck in the same queue for entry-level accounting jobs, and I owe 41,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's in September, apply to maybe 40 small local firms by post and phone, not online forms, and keep the pharmacy shifts. I'd ask my course tutor to put me in touch with former students. I'd also keep paying only the minimum on the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. It's a flat sort of worry, not a sharp one, like a bill you know is coming but can't pay yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pharmacy job keeps you going. What happens to your money if no job comes by the end of the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If nothing comes by the end of September I'd go full-time at the pharmacy, about 1,300 a month. Rent is 480 in a shared house, so the debt would just sit there. My friend Priya says that's giving up, but I call it eating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all. Is that a choice, even in a world where AI is mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a choice. I've watched classmates paste their essays into chatbots and get marks that don't match what they know. I want to be able to do a bank reconciliation on paper, and I think firms will still want someone who can.

say: I'd say it's good news if it means **people** keep their jobs.
I'd tell colleagues I'm not worried, but only because I don't want the argument.
think: Nothing improves for me, so I'm still facing **few junior jobs** and a big debt.
I resent firms that ask for experience nobody gave me a chance to get.
do: Finish the master's and apply to **40 small firms** by phone and post.
Keep the Saturday pharmacy shifts and pay only the **minimum** on the loan.
Ask my tutor for contacts among former students.
feel: A flat, steady **worry** about debt, not a sharp fear.
S0.quote: Hype or not, I'm still stuck in the same queue for entry-level accounting jobs, and I owe 41,000.
fieldNote: Resistant to **AI** by habit and principle; she links it to firms' bad hiring, not to the technology.
Already carries **debt** and a thin cushion, so even a quiet world is stressful.
Distrusts online application systems and prefers phone and post.

steps.text: Keep working Saturdays at the pharmacy counter
Phone 40 small Bradford accounting firms by September
Ask my tutor to connect me with former students

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it needs rules. If firms hand the checking and data entry to software, there have to be protections for the people they stop hiring. At the student union I'd push for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is my exact moment. Reconciling, invoice checking and tax forms are the jobs they give to a graduate in year one, and those are the jobs AI takes. I never learned the tools, so I'm worried I'm the person left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to learn at least the basics, which I hate admitting. I'd ask my tutor Mr. Okafor to show me what firms use, spend two evenings a week on it, and look for work in audit or payroll where there's still a person signing things off. And I'd join the graduate section of a union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, a bit angry. Everything I trained for is being cut up and handed to a machine before I've had a single full-time pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in a junior accountant's day do you think go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bookkeeping and the checking go first, the stuff where you tick and match things for hours. What's left is talking to clients and judging, and nobody lets a new graduate do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the entry-level jobs thin out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big firms, and honestly the government for letting them. The big firms made the entry-level ladder, they're sawing it off, and young people carry the cost. A regulation that makes them keep training graduates would be fair.

say: I'd say firms need **rules** to protect the people they stop hiring.
I'd push for it through the student union.
think: Junior tasks like **reconciling and invoice checks** are exactly what goes first, and I have no work experience.
I'm afraid I'm too slow with technology and will be left behind.
do: Ask my tutor to show me what **firms really use**, then practise two evenings a week.
Aim for audit or payroll roles where a person still signs off.
Join the graduate section of a **union**.
feel: **Frightened** and angry that the entry-level ladder is being cut.
S1.quote: The big firms made the entry-level ladder, they're sawing it off, and young people carry the cost.
fieldNote: Blame lands on **big firms** and government, a clear progressive lens.
Reluctant **retraining**: she will learn the basics but resents having to.
**Fear** is specific: first-year tasks are the ones software takes.

steps.text: Learn the basics of firms' audit software with Mr. Okafor
Apply for payroll and audit roles where people still sign off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and nobody is telling the truth about it. At the student union I'd say we need an emergency plan, money for people whose jobs vanish, and a freeze on cutting graduate hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm finished before I start. The finance jobs are all thinking work, and there's no second path for me because I'm doing a master's in the thing that goes first. And I owe 41,000 on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I have no plan. I'd keep the pharmacy job because robots for hands-on work are three years behind, and I'd stop the master's if I could get the fees back. I'd go and sit with my mum and work out who can pay what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Close to panic. It's like the floor is being pulled away and I can't even see where to stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would you say to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum, who cleans offices at night, that I'm sorry, because she scraped to get me to university. And that I'd keep working at the pharmacy so we don't lose the rent. I'd cry a bit first. My mum cleans offices at night and scraped to get me to university, and now my degree might be worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay people a basic income while this settles and cancel student debt for anyone who studied what the machines now do. Make the companies that win from this pay in. I'd vote for anyone who promised that.

say: I'd say we're **not ready** and need an emergency plan.
I'd demand income support and a **freeze** on cutting graduate hiring.
think: My degree could be **worthless** before I have ever used it in a real job.
I have no second path and owe **41,000**.
do: Keep the **pharmacy job**, since hands-on work lasts longer.
Ask whether I can stop the master's and get fees back.
Sit down with my mum and **list every bill**.
feel: Close to **panic**, like the floor is going.
S2.quote: My mum cleans offices at night and scraped to get me to university, and now my degree might be worth nothing.
fieldNote: Two years leaves **no room**: no savings, no plan, no technology habit.
Her fear is for her **mother** as much as herself.
Turns to **political demands** because she has no personal levers.

steps.text: Keep every Saturday shift at the pharmacy counter
Ask the university whether I can leave and get fees back
Vote for parties promising income support and debt cancellation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to fight for something, if we start now. Unions, the government, universities, everybody needs a plan for what happens to people like us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still scared, but I can breathe. Five years takes me through to 2031, and I could clear some debt first, but I'd guess accountancy is gone by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take whatever first job I can, even in payroll or at a charity, and live very cheaply. I'd throw everything at the loan, maybe 250 a month. I'd also learn the AI tools, because by then I think refusing would be like refusing email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but with a bit of hope. It's the first scenario where I can picture a plan on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different for you with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get a job at all, honestly. Even a bad job gives me a payslip and a way to pay down debt. Two years would not have given me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use them to build one skill a firm can't easily copy, like talking to nervous small business owners about their money. And I'd back a union campaign for a retraining fund funded by the firms that automate.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to fight** if we start now.
I'd want unions and universities to agree a plan for graduates.
think: I can breathe a little, but **accountancy** is probably gone by then.
I'd have time to clear some **debt** first.
do: Take any first job, even **payroll or a charity**, and live cheaply.
Pay about **250 a month** towards the loan.
Learn AI tools, because refusing will be like refusing email.
feel: Scared but with some **hope**, because a plan is possible.
S3.quote: Five years takes me through to 2031, and I could clear some debt first, but I'd guess accountancy is gone by then.
fieldNote: The extra time softens **panic** into planning, but her mood stays high because of the debt.
First time she would use **AI tools**, and only when forced by time.
Wants **collective** solutions funded by the firms that automate.

steps.text: Take any first job, even payroll or charity work
Put 250 a month towards the student loan
Learn the AI tools firms use for bookkeeping
Back a union campaign for a retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it on your course, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we should use it properly: retraining funds, shorter weeks, a safety net before anything breaks. I'd write to my MP and talk about it on the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm 34. I'd have a different job, probably something with people, and the debt would be mostly gone. I still worry the people at the top won't share any of it, but I'm less worried about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, get a first job, even a poor one, then spend a few evenings a year learning a second trade. Something with clients, like helping tenants or small shops with their accounts. I'd probably still keep AI at arm's length, but I'd learn what it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot calmer. It's a normal worry about debt and rent, not the floor going away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still work in accounting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe part of it, in a charity or a council, where there's a person at the desk because it's a public job. But I wouldn't count on it, and I'd teach myself a second thing just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell younger students starting this degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take your time, do an internship even if it's unpaid for a month, and join a union early. Ten years is long enough to change course twice, so don't take huge loans for one narrow path like I did.

say: I'd say ten years is a gift and we should build a **safety net**.
I'd write to my local MP and raise it on the course.
think: By 34 I'd have a different **job**, probably working with people.
I worry the people at the top won't share the **gains**.
do: Get any **first job**, then spend evenings learning a second trade.
Learn what AI does, even if I keep it at arm's length.
Write to my MP about **retraining funds**.
feel: Much **calmer**, an ordinary worry about debt and rent.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to change course twice, so don't take huge loans for one narrow path like I did.
fieldNote: Time lets her imagine a **second career** with people, a progressive and public-minded one.
She still holds **AI** at arm's length, the resistant trait showing even here.
**Debt** and a thin cushion keep her at anxious, not calm.

steps.text: Get any first job, then study a second trade in the evenings
Apply to charities and councils with front desk roles
Write to my MP about retraining funds

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years worries me most, because I'd have no time and no savings, and my mum would pay for my mistake. What would help is income support, debt relief for people my age, and rules that make firms keep training graduates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss if it all went. I'd miss the feeling of balancing a set of books by hand, when the last number finally agrees. It sounds silly, but I picked this because I liked it.

headlineQuote: I'd miss the feeling of balancing a set of books by hand, when the last number finally agrees.
portrait: Daria is a **24-year-old** master's student in management accounting in Bradford, with no internship and heavy debt.
She holds a **progressive** view: blames big firms and government and wants unions, regulation and income support.
She is **resistant** to AI tools and avoids them, so entry-level automation frightens her most.
Her mood climbs from anxious to **panicked** with the 2-year warning, and eases a little with more time.
She works Saturdays at a **pharmacy** and her mother cleans offices, so there is no family cushion.
biggestWorry: Daria fears the **2-year** scenario most, because she'd have no time, savings or plan, and her mum would suffer.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **income support**, debt relief and rules forcing firms to keep training graduates.
